summary: This is the solution-treated (as-quenched) reference state of the Ni-containing duplex low-density steel Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.8C-5Ni (wt.%), one of two alloys (the other being the Ni-free Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.8C) used in the paper to evaluate the nano-mechanical properties of Fe-Mn-Al-C lightweight steels. The alloy was induction-melted, then solution heat-treated for 35 min at 1250 °C under protective argon and water quenched, giving a duplex austenite (γ) + ferrite (α) microstructure without ordered precipitates. Its nano-hardness — 4.2 GPa for γ and 3.1 GPa for α — serves as the baseline against which the annealed, precipitate-bearing states (κ-carbide and B2) of the same alloy are compared.
composition: Nominal composition of the experimental alloy is Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.8C-5Ni (all in wt.%), i.e. an iron-based duplex low-density steel containing 15 wt.% Mn, 10 wt.% Al, 0.8 wt.% C and 5 wt.% Ni. Mn and Al are the principal alloying additions that lower the mass density relative to conventional steels, Al also acting as a ferrite (α) stabiliser; C and Mn promote the formation of ordered κ-carbide in austenite, and Ni is deliberately added so that the B2 intermetallic that forms is NiAl-type rather than FeAl-type, since Ni-Al bonds are stronger than Fe-Al bonds. The paper's alloy tables label this grade as Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.5C-5Ni (0.5 C), whereas the abstract, introduction, results and methods give 0.8 C; this appears to be a typographical inconsistency in the carbon content.
processing: The alloy was first melted in an induction furnace. The defining process of this sample is the solution heat treatment: the material was held for 35 min at 1250 °C in a protective argon atmosphere and then water quenched, producing the as-quenched 'Solution Treated' state studied here. The solution-treated material was then cut into 3-mm (length) × 3-mm (width) × 1-mm (thickness) specimens for testing. This state is the precursor to the isothermal annealing treatments of the same alloy at 500 °C, 700 °C, 900 °C and 1050 °C; it is also the reference used in the nano-indentation arrays that mapped the individual γ and α phases and their phase combinations.
microstructure: In the solution-treated (as-quenched) condition the Ni-containing Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.8C-5Ni alloy has a duplex austenite (γ) + ferrite (α) microstructure, described as the bulk γ and α phases measured without ordered precipitates (two phases, no κ-carbide or B2 in the as-quenched state). No grain size, texture, volume fraction or defect data are reported for this specific condition. The paper's microstructural framework, established in the authors' previous study on the same grades, shows that ordered phases develop only on subsequent annealing: from 900 to 1050 °C B2 appears as micron-sized particles and grain-boundary precipitates in austenite and as nano-sized (~200 nm) discs in ferrite (NiAl-type in the Ni-containing grade), whereas from 500 to 700 °C nano-sized cuboidal κ (<100 nm) forms in austenite and, in the Ni-containing grade, the entire α phase is progressively replaced by B2 stringer bands instead of the needle-like κ seen in the Ni-free grade. The B2 phase thus exists at two length scales — micron-sized particles/stringers in γ and nano-sized discs in α — while κ appears as nano-sized blocks in γ.
properties: Nano-indentation was performed at room temperature on 3-mm × 3-mm × 1-mm specimens at a constant loading/unloading rate of 500 μN s−1 up to a maximum load of 10000 μN with a 20 s hold; each phase was measured at least 25 times in arrays of 50–70 indentations. For the solution-treated Ni-containing alloy the nano-hardness is 4.2 GPa for the γ (austenite) phase and 3.1 GPa for the α (ferrite) phase; the text quotes the same values approximately as ≈4 GPa (γ) and ≈3 GPa (α). These are the parent-phase values against which all precipitate-bearing composites are compared: γ + κ 6.7–7.5 GPa, γ + κ + B2 8.8–9 GPa, γ + B2 7.9–8.2 GPa, α + B2 11.7–13.5 GPa and B2 stringer bands 10.1–10.6 GPa for the same alloy after annealing. The corresponding load–depth curves (Fig. 4a,c) rise to a flat plateau at ≈10000 µN reached at depths of roughly 200–310 nm, with near-vertical unloading branches. No tensile, fatigue, creep, physical, chemical or radiation properties are reported for this sample. Characterization techniques applied across the study were field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) with X-ray energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS, Carl Zeiss Sigma, 20 kV, specimens polished and etched in 5% nital), transmission electron microscopy (TEM; JEOL 2000FX; selected-area diffraction patterns and bright-field imaging; twin-jet electro-polished foils in 10% perchloric acid + 90% ethanol at 25 V), nano-indentation, and first-principles DFT calculations (Quantum-ESPRESSO) of the ordered κ-carbide and FeAl-B2 phases.
mechanisms: Solution treatment at 1250 °C for 35 min in argon followed by water quenching retains a fully duplex austenite + ferrite microstructure free of ordered precipitates, so the as-quenched γ and α phases represent the bulk matrix properties prior to any precipitation.

Because nano-indentation cannot resolve isolated nano-sized precipitates, the measured values are compound (matrix + particle) hardness values, and any change of indenter size or applied load would introduce a nano-indentation size effect from the varying size and shape of the plastic zone, which could obscure the true contribution of each precipitate.

The higher hardness of α + B2 composites (e.g. 11.7 GPa at 900 °C and 13.5 GPa at 1050 °C) than of the parent α phase (~3 GPa) is attributed to the Orowan mechanism: the increase in shear stress Δτ scales inversely with precipitate diameter (Δτ ∝ R^−1.25), so the uniformly dispersed nano-sized B2 discs raise the shear resistance of the α matrix.

Adding Ni increases the hardness of B2 because the intermetallic becomes NiAl-type instead of FeAl-type; Ni-Al bonds are stronger than Fe-Al bonds, and the enthalpy of formation of B2-(Fe,Ni)1−x-Alx becomes increasingly more negative as Fe is replaced by Ni (DFT comparative elastic constants also give higher C11 and C44 for Ni-Al than for Fe-Al compounds).

Hardness of the Ni-containing B2 phase is a function of its Ni content: Ni atoms preferentially accumulate in the α phase to form B2 stringer bands at the low annealing temperatures (500–700 °C), leaving less Ni for the nano-B2 discs at high temperature; with increasing annealing temperature more Ni is available in the nano-sized B2, raising hardness from 9.1 GPa (Ni 8.2 wt.%) at 500 °C to 10.5 GPa (Ni 10.1 wt.%) at 1050 °C, matching the monotonic increase seen in the nano-disk B2 hardness.

In the κ-carbide, substituting Fe by Mn increases the lattice parameter (3.78 Å for Fe2MnAlC to 3.84 Å for Mn3AlC, reflecting the larger Mn radius, rMn = 1.61 Å versus rFe = 1.56 Å) and raises all elastic constants; DFT shows the C11, bulk modulus, shear modulus and Young's modulus of Mn3AlC exceed those of Fe3AlC, so κ particles richer in Mn (e.g. ≈24.8 wt.% at 700 °C versus ≈18.4 wt.% at 500 °C) are harder, consistent with the measured α + κ hardness increase.

The insertion of C into the octahedral interstitial site rigidifies the Fe3AlC (L1'2) κ structure relative to Fe3Al through strong Fe–C bonds along <100>, giving Fe3AlC the largest bulk modulus and shear modulus among the Fe-Al and Fe-Al-C phases and a marked elastic anisotropy (Cα = 2.39 from the acoustic method and 2.47 from the lattice-distortion method), which is why E111 is smaller than E100 for this phase.
The high elastic anisotropy of the κ phase also rationalises its morphology: nano-sized cuboidal κ in γ and needle-like κ in α, as confirmed by phase-field modelling and experiment.

Solid-solution hardening/free-energy arguments explain why the highest-temperature precipitation is hardest: higher annealing temperature changes the formation energy, lattice parameter and magnetization of the κ phase and increases the Ni content of B2, both of which raise the intrinsic hardness of the precipitate.

κ-carbide is less resistant to shear than B2, yet adding brittle nano-sized κ to a γ + micron-sized B2 composite still raises the measured hardness (γ + κ + B2, 8.8–9 GPa, is harder than γ + micron-sized B2 alone), because the κ blocks add further resistance to shear of the austenitic matrix.
conclusions: The solution-treated Ni-containing Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.8C-5Ni steel provides the baseline nano-mechanical state of the study: a duplex γ + α microstructure with γ = 4.2 GPa and α = 3.1 GPa, measured by nano-indentation. Within the paper, this as-quenched reference shows that the Ni-containing alloy's parent phases are only slightly harder than those of the Ni-free Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.8C grade (γ ≈ 4.0 GPa, α ≈ 3.0 GPa), the significant hardness gains appearing only after annealing and the associated precipitation of κ-carbide and B2. The paper's central conclusions, benchmarked against this baseline, are that (i) Ni addition raises B2 hardness because NiAl-type B2 replaces FeAl-type B2, increasing peak hardness from 7.2 GPa to 9 GPa in both austenite and ferrite; (ii) in the Ni-containing alloy the ferrite annealed at 900–1050 °C forms a hard ~10 GPa structure through dispersion of NiAl nano-sized B2 discs; (iii) nano-sized cuboid κ plus micron-sized B2 formed in austenite at ≤700 °C further hardens γ, whereas γ annealed at 900–1050 °C is softer because the nano-sized cuboid κ is unstable; and (iv) DFT confirms that interstitial C enhances the elastic constants of the κ (L1'2) phase and that Mn substitution in Fe3AlC-κ further stiffens it, in agreement with experiment. The main methodological caveat is that nano-indentation cannot measure isolated nano-sized precipitates, so only compound matrix + particle values were obtained for those features, and the properties of nano-sized κ had to be evaluated through first-principles calculation instead.
unmapped: Tables 1 and 2 label the Ni-containing alloy as Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.5C-5Ni (0.5 C), whereas the abstract, introduction, results and methods give Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.8C-5Ni (0.8 C); this appears to be a typographical inconsistency in the carbon content.

The paper notes that the nano-indentation technique as performed measures the hardness of nano-sized features within their surrounding matrix (a compound matrix + particle value) and that changing the indentation size or volume would introduce a nano-indentation size effect — a stated methodological limitation relevant to all indentation-derived values including those of the solution-treated state.

Broader DFT results reported for the ordered compounds (not specific to this solution-treated sample) include: the calculated lattice parameter of ordered FeAl-B2 (with and without spin effects) is slightly below the experimental value but in good agreement; the Fe3AlC lattice constant is larger than that of Fe3Al; the L1'2 Fe3AlC ground state favours the ferromagnetic state by 30 meV/at with a magnetic moment of 1.1 μB/at.Fe (less than half that of Fe3Al), the reduction being attributed to Fe-C interactions rather than to the lattice expansion; the four κ-carbides (Fe3AlC, Fe2MnAlC, FeMn2AlC, Mn3AlC) have nearly identical DOS shapes differing only by a rigid band shift; and the phonon dispersions show an optical gap of about 0.7 THz between Al-derived high-frequency and Fe-derived low-frequency branches in FeAl and Fe3AlC but a gapless, dynamically stable spectrum for Fe3Al.
